 Global health authorities are expected to announce that the U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health milestone it achieved 26 years ago. This past year, the number of cases in the U.S. doubled, making it the worst year in three decades. That was the focus of the latest episode of Horizons with William Brangham. 
 Read the Full Transcript
 Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors. 
 Amna Nawaz: 
 Well, global health authorities are expected to announce tomorrow that the U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health milestone it achieved 26 years ago. This past year, the number of cases in the U.S. doubled, making it the worst year in three decades.
 That was the focus of our newest episode of "Horizons" with William Brangham. Here's part of that discussion.
 William Brangham: 
 Dr. Schaffner, I'm curious. If someone is hearing all of this, worried about perhaps this very big undercount of measles, if they get vaccinated, how much protection does that offer you? Is this a bulletproof, 100 percent protection? How much does it give you?
 Dr. William Schaffner: 
 It's close to bulletproof. It's among the best vaccines we have. If you take the two recommended doses, you will get somewhere between 97 and 98 percent likelihood of protection for the rest of your life.
 And even if you do happen to get a breakthrough infection, namely, you're exposed -- you're vaccinated, you're exposed, and you still get an infection, your illness will be milder. So this is a terrific vaccine in terms of effectiveness, and it's also terrifically safe.
 There are very few adverse events associated with this vaccine. It's been used in the literal billions of doses around the world for 50 years now.
 William Brangham: 
 Jessica Malaty Rivera, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., plays a complicated role here. At times, when asked about measles outbreaks, he has said, yes, go get vaccinated, it will protect you.
 But in his previous career and in his current role in the federal government, he has done an enormous amount to sow distrust about vaccines and say that they are dangerous, they are harming people, that the government is not being square with people about this. How much responsibility do you place at the leadership of the federal government right now?
 Jessica Malaty Rivera: 
 I think he and the federal government bear a huge amount of responsibility because I think that this movement or this unprecedented outbreak didn't necessarily start at the beginning of it.
 There were seeds that were planted years and years ago by RFK Jr. himself and by people from his organization, his former organization, Children's Health Defense, and many like both of those actors who were sowing seeds of doubt about the MMR vaccine safety, the MMR vaccine's effectiveness, even the MMR vaccine's utility.
 And I think he would even say today that the only way to prevent the virus, the infection, is through the MMR vaccine. But what he's also saying is that it's OK to get it and it's OK to suffer for it because it's just a mild disease.
 And this is where I think that the normalization of disease has become so ubiquitous among people who are anti-MMR vaccine, because they have been sold a lie. They have been sold a lie that it is something that can be treated with vitamin A, and it cannot, that it's something that is typical for childhood, when I'm grateful that I live in a time where my children don't have to experience a disease that was so prevalent back in the '80s.
 Even varicella is an example of that we have the tools to prevent them. Suffering can be avoided. It should not be the expectation simply because there are ways in which you could care for somebody. Now, it's also important to note there is no known specific treatment for measles. It's all supportive care.
 And some kids will get pneumonia. And pneumonia is the number one cause of measles-related death. Some kids may get encephalitis. That is a very dangerous swelling of the brain that can cause a lot of permanent damage, including hearing loss and blindness and other impairments. It can cause complications years after recovery and a rare encephalitis called SSPE.
 It can cause immune amnesia. These are not benign complications of a disease that is almost nearly entirely preventable through two doses of that vaccine. And RFK Jr. absolutely knows this. And it is the responsibility of the administration and our HHS secretary to make it extremely clear that kids do not have to be getting a very preventable disease.
 Amna Nawaz: 
 And you can watch that full episode of "Horizons" and more on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.
